issues.legal_issue: A landlord may enforce a permission to evict that became final under the former rent-control law through an application under the successor law even if a suit based on that permission was filed and dismissed on a technical ground.
material_facts: Permission to seek eviction was granted under the former law and became final after a revision was rejected.
The landlord filed a suit relying on that permission, but the suit was dismissed on a technical ground without a decision on the merits.
The landlord then applied for eviction under the successor law, and the application was rejected on the ground that the permission had been exhausted by filing the suit.
The successor law’s transitional provision was amended to apply whether or not a suit had been instituted, and the amendment was retrospective.
issues.conclusion: The application was maintainable. The earlier suit’s technical dismissal did not exhaust the permission or prevent the landlord from seeking eviction under the successor law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 43(2)(rr) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 enabled enforcement of a final permission obtained under section 3 of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947. The 1976 amendment, which applied whether or not a suit had been instituted, operated retrospectively. A permission granted to achieve eviction is not exhausted when that purpose remains unfulfilled and the suit based on it was dismissed on a technical ground. The Court approved Pahlad Das v. Ganga Saran, AIR 1958 Allahabad 774, and referred to D.K. Soni v. P.K. Mukherjee for the importance of finality in judicial proceedings.

rule.if: transitional_eviction_application and final_former_law_permission and prior_suit_dismissed_on_technical_ground and eviction_not_completed

predicates.transitional_eviction_application: A landlord sought eviction through an application under a successor law that provides for enforcement of a final permission obtained under the former law.
predicates.final_former_law_permission: The permission to seek eviction under the former law had become final.
predicates.prior_suit_dismissed_on_technical_ground: The landlord had filed a suit relying on the permission, and the suit was dismissed on a technical ground without a decision on the merits.
predicates.eviction_not_completed: The tenant had not been evicted, so the purpose for which the permission was granted remained unfulfilled.

issues.definition: When a landlord uses the successor-law application process, has a final former-law permission, and an earlier suit based on it ended technically without eviction, the application remains maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: A technical defect in a lower court’s exercise of appellate authority does not require Supreme Court interference when the High Court, exercising writ jurisdiction, finds the underlying order improper and justice has been done.
material_facts: No appeal lay from the Prescribed Authority’s decision to the District Judge.
The District Judge nevertheless set aside the Prescribed Authority’s decision.
The High Court found the Prescribed Authority’s decision invalid and improper, and declined to interfere with the District Judge’s result while exercising writ jurisdiction.
The matter reached the Supreme Court by special leave, and the Court concluded that the improper decision had been set aside and justice had been done.
issues.conclusion: Despite the technical defect in the District Judge’s exercise of appellate authority, there was no basis for interference under Article 136 because the High Court could itself have set aside the improper decision under Article 226 and justice had been done.
issues.legal_principle: Although no appeal lay to the District Judge, the High Court exercising jurisdiction under Article 226 could itself have set aside the Prescribed Authority’s invalid and improper order. In those circumstances, the Supreme Court found no scope for interference under Article 136. The Court considered Shri Bhagwan v. Ram Chand, [1965] 3 SCR 218, inapplicable to the facts.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and lower_appellate_court_lacked_appeal_authority and underlying_order_improper and high_court_could_set_aside_under_writ

predicates.special_leave_appeal: A party brought the matter before the Supreme Court by special leave.
predicates.lower_appellate_court_lacked_appeal_auth: The lower appellate court set aside an order even though no appeal lay to it.
predicates.underlying_order_improper: The High Court found the original decision invalid and improper.
predicates.high_court_could_set_aside_under_writ: The High Court had writ jurisdiction through which it could itself set aside the original decision.

issues.definition: When a special-leave appeal follows an unauthorized lower appeal, but the original order was improper and the High Court could set it aside under its writ jurisdiction, Supreme Court interference is unwarranted.
